1.pericope_label: God blesses Noah, sets the fear of man on the beasts, and gives every moving thing for food

schools.summary: Gill says God blessed Noah and his sons with temporal blessings, not spiritual ones, for though some of them were blessed with such, yet not all, particularly Ham. The fear and dread of man upon every beast is a renewal, at least in part, of the grant of dominion to Adam over all the creatures, Gill says: these obeyed him cheerfully and from love, but sinning, he in a good measure lost his power over them and they rebelled against him; now, though the charter of power over them is renewed, they do not serve man freely but are in dread of him and flee from him, some being more easily brought into subjection, and even the fiercest and wildest may be tamed. This power over them was the more easily retrieved in all probability by Noah and his sons, Gill adds, from the inhabitation of the creatures with them for so long a time in the ark. Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you means every beast, fowl and fish without exception, Gill says, for though there was a difference at this time of clean and unclean creatures with respect to sacrifice, yet not with respect to food; every creature of God was good then as it is now, and it was left to man's reason and judgment what to make use of as would be most conducive to his health and agreeable to his taste. Though there was a distinction afterwards made under the Levitical dispensation among the Jews, who were forbidden the use of some creatures, Gill notes that they themselves say all unclean beasts will be clean in the world to come, in the times of the Messiah, as they were to the sons of Noah, and refer to this text in proof of it; the only exception in the text is that they must be living creatures which are taken and used for food, not such as die of themselves or are torn by wild beasts, but such as are taken alive and killed in a proper manner. Calvin says we hence infer with what great fear Noah had been dejected, because God so often and at such length proceeds to encourage him; for when Moses says that God blessed Noah and his sons, he does not simply mean that the favour of fruitfulness was restored to them, but that at the same time the design of God concerning the new restitution of the world was revealed unto them, since to the blessing itself is added the voice of God by which he addresses them. We know that brute animals produce offspring in no other way than by the blessing of God, Calvin says, but Moses here commemorates a privilege which belongs only to men; therefore, lest those four men and their wives, seized with trepidation, should doubt for what purpose they had been delivered, the Lord prescribes to them their future condition of life, namely that they shall raise up mankind from death to life. Thus he not only renews the world by the same word by which he before created it, Calvin says, but he directs his word to men, in order that they may recover the lawful use of marriage, may know that the care of producing offspring is pleasing to himself, and may have confidence that a progeny shall spring from them which shall diffuse itself through all regions of the earth. Yet he did not permit promiscuous intercourse, Calvin adds, but sanctioned anew that law of marriage which he had before ordained; and although the blessing of God is in some way extended to illicit connections, so that offspring is thence produced, yet this is an impure fruitfulness, that which is lawful flowing only from the expressly declared benediction of God. Of the dominion Calvin says that although after the fall of man the beasts were endued with new ferocity, yet some remains of that dominion which God had conferred on him in the beginning were still left, and he now promises that the same dominion shall continue. We see indeed that wild beasts rush violently upon men and rend and tear many of them in pieces, Calvin says, and if God did not wonderfully restrain their fierceness the human race would be utterly destroyed; savage beasts prevail and rage against men in various ways, and no wonder, for since we perversely exalt ourselves against God, why should not the beasts rise up against us. Nevertheless the providence of God is a secret bridle to restrain their violence, he says: whence does it arise that serpents spare us, unless because he represses their virulence, and whence is it that tigers, elephants, lions, bears, wolves and other wild beasts without number do not rend and tear and devour everything human, except that they are withheld by this subjection as by a barrier. The bridle with which the Lord restrains the cruelty of wild beasts is a certain fear and dread which God has implanted in them, Calvin says, to the end that they might reverence the presence of men; and another advantage more widely extended is here noted, namely that men may render animals subservient to their own convenience, so that oxen become accustomed to bear the yoke, the wildness of horses is subdued to carry a rider, cows give milk, and sheep are mute under the hand of the shearer, all these being the result of this dominion, which although greatly diminished is nevertheless not entirely abolished. Of the grant of flesh Calvin says that because Moses now first relates that this right was given to men, nearly all commentators infer that it was not lawful for man to eat flesh before the deluge, but that the natural fruits of the earth were his only food; but the argument is not sufficiently firm, for he holds to this principle, that God here does not bestow on men more than he had previously given, but only restores what had been taken away, that they might again enter on the possession of those good things from which they had been excluded. For since they had before offered sacrifices to God, and were also permitted to kill wild beasts, from the hides and skins of which they might make for themselves garments and tents, Calvin says he does not see what obligation should prevent them from the eating of flesh; but since it is of little consequence what opinion is held, he affirms nothing on the subject. His editor demurs, observing that the question Calvin here dismisses as of little importance has in modern controversy assumed a very different position, that most commentators have come to the reverse decision, and that Calvin's argument appears chargeable with the want of firmness which he imputes to others, since the inference that the flesh of sacrifices was eaten is of no force if the first sacrifices were all whole burnt offerings, and the garments made from skins were in all probability those of the very animals sacrificed. What ought justly to be deemed by us of greater importance, Calvin says, is that to eat the flesh of animals is granted to us by the kindness of God, that we do not seize upon what our appetite desires as robbers do, nor yet tyrannically shed the innocent blood of cattle, but that we only take what is offered to us by the hand of the Lord. Whence has it happened to man that he should eat whatever food he pleased before God with a tranquil mind, and not with unbridled licence, except from his knowing that it has been divinely delivered into his hand by the right of donation? Wherefore, Paul being witness, the word of God sanctifies the creatures that we may purely and lawfully feed on them; and let the adage be utterly rejected which says that no one can feed and refresh his body with a morsel of bread without at the same time defiling his soul.

Matthew Henry says that we read in the close of the foregoing chapter the very kind things which God said in his heart concerning the remnant of mankind now left to be the seed of a new world, and here we have these kind things spoken to them. All God's promises of good flow from his purposes of love and the counsels of his own will, Henry says; and as we read how Noah blessed God by his altar and sacrifice, so here we find God blessing Noah, for God will graciously bless, that is, do well for, those who sincerely bless, that is, speak well of, him. Here we have the Magna Charta, Henry says, the great charter of this new kingdom of nature which was now to be erected and incorporated, the former charter having been forfeited and seized; and the grants of this charter are kind and gracious to men. First is a grant of lands of vast extent and a promise of a great increase of men to occupy and enjoy them: God sets the whole earth before them and tells them it is all their own while it remains, and though it is not a paradise but a wilderness rather, yet it is better than we deserve, and blessed be God it is not hell. He gives them a blessing by the force and virtue of which mankind should be both multiplied and perpetuated upon earth, Henry says, so that in a little time all the habitable parts of the earth should be more or less inhabited, and though one generation should pass away yet another should come, so that the stream of the human race should run parallel with the current of time till both should be delivered up together into the ocean of eternity; though death should still reign, the earth should never again be dispeopled as now it was. Second is a grant of power over the inferior creatures, Henry says, a title to them, into your hands they are delivered, and a dominion over them, without which the title would avail little; this revives a former grant, only with this difference, that man in innocence ruled by love and fallen man rules by fear. This grant remains in force, he says, and thus far we have still the benefit of it, that those creatures which are any way useful to us are reclaimed and we use them either for service or food, the horse and ox patiently submitting to the bridle and yoke and the sheep being dumb both before the shearer and before the butcher, for the fear and dread of man are upon them; and that those creatures that are any way hurtful to us are restrained, so that though now and then man may be hurt by some of them, they do not combine together to rise up in rebellion against man, else God could by these destroy the world as effectually as he did by a deluge. What is it, Henry asks, that keeps wolves out of our towns and lions out of our streets, and confines them to the wilderness, but this fear and dread; nay, some have been tamed. Third is a grant of maintenance and subsistence, Henry says, every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you, whereas hitherto, most think, man had been confined to feed only upon the products of the earth. He adds a caution about the creatures given, that we ought not to abuse them by gluttony, still less by cruelty, nor to pain them needlessly whilst they live, nor when we take away their lives.

Charles Ellicott says the blessing bestowed upon Noah, the second father of mankind, is exactly parallel to that given to our first father, with a significant addition growing out of the history of the past: there is the same command to fill the world with human life and the same promise that the fear of man shall rest upon the whole animated creation, but this grant of dominion is so extended that the animals are now given to man for his food. But just as there was a restriction as regards Adam's food, the fruit of the tree of knowledge being refused him, Ellicott says, so now there is a prohibition against the eating of blood; and the addition is the sanctity given to human life, with the evident object of guarding against such a disruption of the human race as was the result of Cain's murder of Abel. Thus man starts afresh upon his task of subjugating the earth, Ellicott concludes, with increased empire over the animal world and with his own life more solemnly guarded and made secure. Keil and Delitzsch say that the words, every moving thing that liveth shall be food for you, even as the green of the herb have I given you all things, do not affirm that man then first began to eat animal food, but only that God then for the first time authorised, or allowed him to do, what probably he had previously done in opposition to his will. The prohibition that follows applies to the eating of flesh with blood in it, Keil says, because the soul of the animal is in the blood, whether of living animals, as is the barbarous custom in Abyssinia, or of slaughtered animals from which the blood has not been drained.

Adam Clarke sets out the argument of the chapter, that God blesses Noah and his sons, that the brute creation is to be subject to them through fear, the first grant of animal food, the eating of blood forbidden, cruelty to animals forbidden, a man-slayer to forfeit his life, the covenant established, the rainbow given as its sign and pledge, the three sons peopling the earth, Noah's vineyard and intoxication, the conduct of Ham and the carriage of Shem and Japheth, the prophecy of the servitude of Ham's posterity and the dignity of Shem and Japheth, and the age and death of Noah. Even the increase of families, which appears to depend on merely natural means and sometimes fortuitous circumstances, is all of God, Clarke says. Prior to the fall man ruled the inferior animals by love and kindness, for then gentleness and docility were their principal characteristics; after the fall, untractableness with savage ferocity prevailed among almost all orders of the brute creation, and enmity to man seems particularly to prevail, so that had not God in his mercy impressed their minds with the fear and terror of man, the human race would long ere this have been totally destroyed by the beasts of the field. Did the horse know his own strength, Clarke asks, and the weakness of the miserable wretch who unmercifully rides, drives, whips, goads and oppresses him, would he not with one stroke of his hoof destroy his tyrant possessor? But while God hides these things from him he impresses his mind with the fear of his owner, so that either by cheerful or sullen submission he is trained up for and employed in the most useful purposes, and even willingly submits when tortured for the sport and amusement of his more brutish oppressor. Tigers, wolves, lions and hyenas, the determinate foes of man, incapable of being tamed or domesticated, flee through the principle of terror from the dwelling of man, and thus he is providentially safe, Clarke says; how wise and gracious is this order of the Divine providence. Of the grant of food Clarke says there is no positive evidence that animal food was ever used before the flood, that Noah had the first grant of this kind, and that it has been continued to all his posterity ever since. It is not likely that this grant would have been now made, Clarke argues, if some extraordinary alteration had not taken place in the vegetable world, so as to render its productions less nutritive than they were before, and probably such a change in the constitution of man as to render a grosser and higher diet necessary; we may therefore safely infer that the earth was less productive after the flood than before, and that the human constitution was greatly impaired by the alterations which had taken place through the whole economy of nature. Morbid debility, induced by an often unfriendly state of the atmosphere with sore and long-continued labour, would necessarily require a higher nutriment than vegetables could supply, Clarke says, and that this was the case appears sufficiently clear from the grant of animal food, which, had it not been indispensably necessary, had not been made; that the constitution of man was then much altered appears in the greatly contracted lives of those after the flood. John Wesley says God assured them of his good-will to them and his gracious intentions concerning them, and that the first blessing is here renewed and repeated, for the race of mankind was as it were to begin again. He grants them power over the inferior creatures, Wesley says, a title to them, into your hands they are delivered, for your use and benefit, and a dominion over them, without which the title would avail little; this revives a former grant, only with this difference, that man in innocency ruled by love and fallen man rules by fear. Hitherto man had been confined to feed only upon the products of the earth, fruits, herbs and roots, and all sorts of corn and milk, Wesley says, but the flood having perhaps washed away much of the virtue of the earth, and so rendered its fruits less pleasing and less nourishing, God now enlarged the grant and allowed man to eat flesh, which perhaps man himself never thought of till now. The Jewish doctors speak so often of the seven precepts of Noah, Wesley notes, which they say were to be observed by all nations, that it may not be amiss to set them down: against the worship of idols; against blasphemy, and requiring to bless the name of God; against murder; against incest and all uncleanness; against theft and rapine; requiring the administration of justice; and against eating flesh with the life. But the precepts here given all concern the life of man, Wesley says, for man must not prejudice his own life by eating that food which is unwholesome and prejudicial to his health.

debates: Whether animal food was first permitted here: Clarke says there is no positive evidence that it was ever used before the flood and that Noah had the first grant; Wesley says man had hitherto been confined to the products of the earth; Keil takes a middle position, that the words authorise for the first time what man had probably been doing already against God's will; Calvin denies the inference altogether, holding that God restores rather than bestows, since men already sacrificed and killed beasts for hides, and then declares the question of little consequence

Why the grant was enlarged just then: Clarke argues that the vegetable world must have become less nutritive and the human constitution impaired, so that a grosser diet became necessary, and points to the contracted lives after the flood; Wesley suspects the flood washed away much of the virtue of the earth; Calvin declines the historical question and presses instead that flesh is to be taken as offered by the hand of the Lord and not seized as robbers do

How the new charter stands to the old: Henry calls it the Magna Charta of a new kingdom of nature, the former charter having been forfeited and seized; Ellicott calls the blessing exactly parallel to Adam's, with the sanctity of human life added against a second Cain, and a new restriction on blood answering to the old restriction on the tree

Why the beasts do not destroy us: Henry, Calvin and Clarke each pose the question rhetorically and answer by the implanted fear, Calvin calling providence a secret bridle on their violence and Clarke turning the case into a charge against cruel owners; Gill adds the homelier reason that the creatures had lived with Noah in the ark so long
outliers: Calvin's editor demurring at Calvin's own argument, that it is chargeable with the want of firmness he imputes to others, since the first sacrifices may all have been whole burnt offerings
Clarke's question whether the horse, knowing his own strength and his rider's weakness, would not destroy his tyrant possessor with one stroke of his hoof
Henry's qualification that the earth granted is a wilderness rather than a paradise, better than we deserve, and blessed be God it is not hell
Henry's caution that we ought not to abuse the creatures by gluttony, still less by cruelty, nor pain them needlessly while they live nor when we take their lives
Wesley's list of the seven precepts of Noah which the Jewish doctors held binding on all nations
Gill's report that the Jews expect all unclean beasts to be clean again in the days of the Messiah, as they were to the sons of Noah, citing this very text

4.pericope_label: Blood forbidden, the life of man required, and whoso sheddeth man’s blood

schools.summary: Gill says this is the only exception to the eating of flesh, that it was not to be eaten with the blood in it, which is said to be its life; not that the blood is of itself the life, but because it is a means of life, and that being exhausted the creature must die, and because the animal and vital spirits appear to us most vigorous in it. Or rather it may be rendered, Gill says, the flesh with its life in its blood, while there is life in the blood, or while the creature is living; the meaning being that a creature designed for food should be properly killed and its blood let out, that it should not be devoured alive as by a beast of prey, and that raw flesh should not be eaten, as since by cannibals and as might have been before the flood. Of the following verse Gill says it is a reason of the preceding law, to teach men not to shed human blood, for though God had given them liberty to slay the creatures and shed their blood and eat them, yet he did not allow them to shed their own blood or the blood of their fellow creatures, and should they do this he would surely make inquisition and punish them for it. Whoso sheddeth man's blood, Gill says, means that he who is guilty of wilful murder shall surely be put to death by the order of the civil magistrate, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, that by witnesses the judges shall condemn him to death; for this is but the law of retaliation, a just and equitable one, blood for blood, or life for life. It seems to be the first law of this kind that empowered the civil magistrate to take away life, Gill says, God, as it is thought, reserving the right and power to himself before, and which for some reasons he thought fit not to make use of in the case of Cain, whom he only banished and suffered not others to take away his life, but now enacts a law requiring judges to punish murder with death, which according to this law ought never to go unpunished, or have a lesser punishment inflicted for it. Calvin says that some explain the passage as meaning, ye may not eat a member cut off from a living animal, which is too trifling; since there is no copulative conjunction between the two words, he does not doubt that Moses, speaking of the life, added the word blood exegetically, as if he would say that flesh is in some sense devoured with its life when it is eaten imbued with its own blood. Wherefore the life and the blood are not put for different things but for the same, Calvin says, not because blood is in itself the life, but inasmuch as the vital spirits chiefly reside in the blood it is, as far as our feeling is concerned, a token which represents life; and this is expressly declared in order that men may have the greater horror of eating blood, for if it be a savage and barbarous thing to devour lives or to swallow down living flesh, men betray their brutality by eating blood. Moreover the tendency of this prohibition is by no means obscure, Calvin says, namely that God intends to accustom men to gentleness by abstinence from the blood of animals, but that if they should become unrestrained and daring in eating wild animals they would at length not be sparing of even human blood. Yet we must remember that this restriction was part of the old law, Calvin adds; wherefore what Tertullian relates, that in his time it was unlawful among Christians to taste the blood of cattle, savours of superstition, for the apostles, in commanding the Gentiles to observe this rite for a short time, did not intend to inject a scruple into their consciences, but only to prevent the liberty which was otherwise sacred from proving an occasion of offence to the ignorant and the weak. In the words that follow, Calvin says, the Lord more explicitly declares that he does not forbid the use of blood out of regard to animals themselves, but because he accounts the life of men precious, and because the sole end of his law is to promote the exercise of common humanity between them; and he dismisses as frivolous the distinction by which the Jews constitute four kinds of homicide, holding the simple and genuine sense to be that God so highly estimates our life that he will not suffer murder to go unavenged. It is no common proof of God's love towards us, Calvin says, that he undertakes the defence of our lives and declares that he will be the avenger of our death; and in saying that he will exact punishment from animals for the violated life of men he gives us this as an example, for if on behalf of man he is angry with brute creatures who are hurried by a blind impulse to feed upon him, what will become of the man who unjustly, cruelly and contrary to the sense of nature falls upon his brother. Of the clause in man Calvin says some expound it, before witnesses, and others refer it to what follows, that by man his blood should be shed, which is the interpretation of the English version, but all these interpretations are forced; the language rather expresses the atrociousness of the crime, because whosoever kills a man draws down upon himself the blood and life of his brother. On the whole, Calvin says, they are deceived in his judgment who think that a political law for the punishment of homicides is here simply intended; he does not deny that the punishments which the laws ordain and the judges execute are founded on this divine sentence, but the words are more comprehensive, for it is written that men of blood shall not live out half their days, and we see some die in highways, some in stews and many in wars. Therefore, however magistrates may connive at the crime, God sends executioners from other quarters who shall render unto sanguinary men their reward, Calvin says, and he so threatens and denounces vengeance against the murderer that he even arms the magistrate with the sword for the avenging of slaughter. For the greater confirmation of this doctrine God declares that he is not thus solicitous respecting human life rashly and for no purpose, Calvin adds: men are indeed unworthy of God's care if respect be had only to themselves, but since they bear the image of God engraven on them he deems himself violated in their person; thus, although they have nothing of their own by which they obtain the favour of God, he looks upon his own gifts in them, and is thereby excited to love and to care for them. This doctrine is to be carefully observed, Calvin says, that no one can be injurious to his brother without wounding God himself, and were it deeply fixed in our minds we should be much more reluctant than we are to inflict injuries; and should any one object that this divine image has been obliterated, the solution is easy, first that there yet exists some remnant of it, so that man is possessed of no small dignity, and secondly that the Celestial Creator himself, however corrupted man may be, still keeps in view the end of his original creation.

Matthew Henry says the main reason of forbidding the eating of blood doubtless was because the shedding of blood in sacrifices was to keep the worshippers in mind of the great atonement, yet it seems intended also to check cruelty, lest men, being used to shed and feed upon the blood of animals, should grow unfeeling to them and be less shocked at the idea of shedding human blood. Man must not take away his own life, Henry says: our lives are God's, and we must only give them up when he pleases, and if we in any way hasten our own death we are accountable to God for it. When God requires the life of a man from him that took it away unjustly, Henry says, the murderer cannot render that, and therefore must render his own instead; one time or other, in this world or in the next, God will discover murders, and punish those murders which are beyond man's power to punish. But there are those who are ministers of God to protect the innocent, by being a terror to evil-doers, and they must not bear the sword in vain, Henry says, and wilful murder ought always to be punished with death. To this law there is a reason added, he concludes: such remains of God's image are still upon fallen man that he who unjustly kills a man defaces the image of God and does dishonour to him.

Charles Ellicott says the words are remarkable, only flesh in its soul, its blood, ye shall not eat, and that the Authorised Version is probably right in taking blood as in apposition to soul, which word means here the principle of animation, or that which causes an animal to live. This is God's especial gift, Ellicott says, for he alone can bestow upon that aggregation of solids and fluids which we call a body the secret principle of life; of this hidden life the blood is the representative, and while man is permitted to have the body for his food, as being the mere vessel which contains this life, the gift itself must go back to God, and the blood as its symbol be treated with reverence. The next verse he would translate, and surely your blood, which is for your souls, will I require, from every beast will I require it, and from man, even from a man's brother will I require the soul of man, as from Cain; your blood, which is for your souls, meaning that it is the means for the maintenance of the animal life within them. As it is the support of man's life, Ellicott says, an animal which sheds it becomes guilty and must be slain, and still more must those animals be destroyed which prey upon man; thus there is a command given for the extirpation of the carnivora at the time when the more peaceful animals had just been saved. The last clause has nothing to do with the avenger of blood, Ellicott insists: the near kinsman is here the murderer, and the commandment requires that even such a one should not be spared. Of the sixth verse he says this penalty of life for life is not to be left to natural law, but man himself, in such a manner and under such safeguards as the civil law in each country shall order, is to execute the Divine command; and thus protected from violence both of man and beast, and with all such terrible crimes forbidden as had polluted Adam's beginning, Noah in peace and security is to commence afresh man's great work upon earth. Keil and Delitzsch say the prohibition applies to the eating of flesh with blood in it, because the soul of the animal is in the blood, whether of living animals, as is the barbarous custom in Abyssinia, or of slaughtered animals from which the blood has not been drained.

Adam Clarke says that though animal food was granted, the blood was most solemnly forbidden, because it was the life of the beast, and this life was to be offered to God as an atonement for sin; hence the blood was ever held sacred, because it was the grand instrument of expiation and because it was typical of that blood by which we enter into the holiest. He traces the prohibition through five stages: before the deluge it was not eaten, because animal food was not in use; after the deluge it was prohibited, and being one of the seven Noahic precepts it was not eaten previously to the publication of the Mosaic law; at the giving of the law and at several times during the ministry of Moses the prohibition was solemnly and with awful penalties renewed, so that we may rest assured no blood was eaten previously to the Christian era, nor indeed ever since by the Jewish people; that the prohibition has been renewed under the Christian dispensation can admit of little doubt by any man who dispassionately reads the Acts, where even the Gentile converts are charged to abstain from it on the authority not only of the apostles but of the Holy Ghost, and this, Clarke insists, not for fear of stumbling the converted Jews, which he calls the gloss of theologians, but because it was one of those necessary points from the burden of obedience to which they could not be excused; and this command is still scrupulously obeyed by the oriental Christians and by the whole Greek Church, and why, he asks, because the reasons still subsist. No blood was eaten under the law because it pointed out the blood that was to be shed for the sin of the world, Clarke says, and under the Gospel it should not be eaten because it should ever be considered as representing the blood which has been shed for the remission of sins; and he adds that if the eaters of blood knew that it affords a very crude, almost indigestible and unwholesome ailment, they would not on these physical reasons be so much attached to it. Of the following verse Clarke says the clause about the beast is very obscure, but if taken literally it seems to be an awful warning against cruelty to the brute creation, and from it we may conclude that horse-racers, hare-hunters, bull-baiters and cock-fighters shall be obliged to give an account to God for every creature they have wantonly destroyed; and he notes that instead of the word for beast the Samaritan reads living, that is, any living creature or person, which makes a very good sense and equally forbids cruelty either to men or brutes. Whoever kills a man, unless unwittingly, shall forfeit his own life, Clarke says: taking away the life of another is the highest offence that can be committed against the individual and against society, and the highest punishment a man can suffer for such a crime is the loss of his own life. But as punishment should be ever proportioned to crimes, Clarke argues, the highest punishment due to the highest crime should not be inflicted for a minor offence, since to do so is injustice and cruelty, and serves only to confound the claims of justice and the different degrees of moral turpitude, and to render the profligate desperate; hence the adage so frequent among almost every order of delinquents, that it is as good to be hanged for a sheep as a lamb, which at once marks their desperation and the injustice of those penal laws which inflict the highest punishment for almost every species of crime. When shall a wise and judicious legislature see the absurdity and injustice of inflicting the punishment of death for stealing a sheep or a horse, or forging a note, and for murdering a man, Clarke asks, when the latter in its moral turpitude and ruinous consequences infinitely exceeds the others; and his publishers append a note that the wish has been realised since the paragraph was written. John Wesley says that blood made atonement for the soul, the life of the sacrifice being accepted for the life of the sinner, so that blood must not be looked upon as a common thing but must be poured out before the Lord; and he adds that Mr Henry has a strange conceit, that this is only a prohibition to eat flesh, which does such apparent violence to the text that to mention it is sufficient. Our own lives are not so our own that we may quit them at our own pleasure, Wesley says, but they are God's, and we must resign them at his pleasure; and to show how tender God was of the life of man, he will have the beast put to death that kills a man, which was confirmed by the law of Moses, and it would not be unsafe to observe it still. At the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of a man means, Wesley says, I will avenge the blood of the murdered upon the murderer, for when God requires the life of a man at the hand of him that took it away unjustly, he cannot render that, and therefore must render his own in lieu of it, which is the only way left of making restitution. Whoso sheddeth man's blood, Wesley adds, whether upon a sudden provocation or premeditated, for rash anger is heart-murder as well as malice prepense, by man shall his blood be shed, that is, by the magistrate or whoever is appointed to be the avenger of blood; before the flood, as it should seem by the story of Cain, God took the punishment of murder into his own hands, but now he committed this judgment to men, to masters of families at first and afterwards to the heads of countries. Man is a creature dear to his Creator and therefore ought to be so to us, Wesley concludes: God put honour upon him, let us not then put contempt upon him, for such remains of God's image are still even upon fallen man that he who unjustly kills a man defaceth the image of God and doth dishonour to him.

debates: Whether the prohibition of blood still binds Christians: Clarke traces it through five stages and holds it renewed under the Gospel on the authority of the Holy Ghost, expressly rejecting as the gloss of theologians the view that it was imposed for fear of stumbling Jewish converts, and notes that the whole Greek Church still obeys it; Calvin holds exactly that rejected view, calling Tertullian's report of Christian abstinence a thing that savours of superstition, since the apostles enjoined it briefly only to keep a sacred liberty from offending the weak

What at the hand of every beast requires: Ellicott finds a command for the extirpation of the carnivora just as the peaceful animals had been saved; Wesley takes it of executing the particular beast that kills a man, and thinks it would not be unsafe to observe still; Clarke reverses the direction and makes it a warning against human cruelty to animals, citing the Samaritan reading living for beast; Calvin makes it an argument from the lesser to the greater about human murder

Whether the sixth verse founds the magistrate's sword: Gill calls it the first law empowering the civil magistrate to take life, God having declined to use that right in the case of Cain, and Wesley and Ellicott agree that the execution is now committed to men and to the civil law of each country; Calvin thinks them deceived who suppose a political law is simply intended, since the words are more comprehensive and God sends executioners from other quarters when magistrates connive

What the phrase in man adds: Calvin rejects both the reading before witnesses and the construction of the English version as forced, holding that the words express the atrociousness of the crime, since whoever kills a man draws his brother's blood down upon himself

Whether the divine image survives to ground the penalty: Calvin meets the objection that it has been obliterated by answering that a remnant yet exists and that the Creator still keeps in view the end of the original creation; Henry and Wesley both say, in the same words, that such remains of God's image are upon fallen man that he who kills defaces it
outliers: Wesley's attack on a fellow commentator by name, that Mr Henry has a strange conceit which does such apparent violence to the text that to mention it is sufficient
Clarke's list of those who must give account for wanton destruction of creatures: horse-racers, hare-hunters, bull-baiters and cock-fighters

Clarke's protest against capital punishment for theft and forgery, with the delinquents' adage that it is as good to be hanged for a sheep as a lamb, and his publishers' note that his wish for reform has since been realised
Clarke's physical postscript that blood affords a very crude, almost indigestible and unwholesome ailment
Calvin's observation that though magistrates connive, God sends executioners from other quarters, so that some die in highways, some in stews and many in wars
Ellicott's insistence that the near kinsman in the last clause is the murderer and not the avenger of blood, so that even he is not to be spared

7.pericope_label: Be fruitful, and the covenant established with Noah, his seed and every living creature

schools.summary: Gill says that instead of taking away the lives of men the great concern should be to multiply them, and that this is indeed one reason of the foregoing law, to prevent the decrease and ruin of mankind, which was peculiarly needful when there were only four men in the world, and therefore it is repeated in stronger terms. Of the covenant Gill says it is not the covenant of grace in Christ, but of the preservation of the creatures in common, a promise that they should not be destroyed any more by a flood, to which promise it seems an oath was annexed, as appears from the passage in Isaiah which refers to this covenant, as Aben Ezra observes; and both to raise attention to what is affirmed and to show the certainty of it, the word behold is prefixed. Nor is it amiss, Gill adds, what Jarchi observes, that this follows upon the direction and exhortation to the procreation of children and is an encouragement to it, since it is assured that posterity should be no more cut off in the manner it had been; for this covenant was made and established not only with Noah and his sons but with all their succeeding offspring. That it is made with every living creature is a further proof, Gill says, that this was not the covenant of grace but of conservation, since it is made with irrational as well as rational creatures; and the repetition of the words is to denote the certainty of it, as well as to lead on to the particulars. Calvin says God again turns his discourse to Noah and his sons, exhorting them to the propagation of offspring, as if he would say, you see that I am intent upon cherishing and preserving mankind, do you therefore also attend to it; at the same time, in commending to them the preservation of seed, he deters them from murder and from unjust acts of violence, though his chief end was to encourage their dejected minds, for in these words is contained not a bare precept but also a promise. That the memory of the deluge might not inspire them with new terrors as often as the sky were covered with clouds, Calvin says, this source of anxiety is taken away; and certainly, if we consider the great propensity of the human mind to distrust, we shall not deem this testimony to have been unnecessary even for Noah, who was indeed endued with a rare and incomparable faith, even to a miracle, but no strength of constancy could be so great that this most sad and terrible vengeance of God should not shake it. Therefore, whenever any great and continued shower shall seem to threaten the earth with a deluge, Calvin says, this barrier on which the holy man may rely is interposed; and although his sons would need this confirmation more than he, yet the Lord speaks especially on his account, the clause about his sons being referred to this point, since God, making his covenant with the sons of Noah, commands them to hope for the best because they are joined with their father, who is as it were the stipulator of the covenant. There is no doubt that it was the design of God to provide for all his posterity, Calvin says: it was not therefore a private covenant confirmed with one family only, but one which is common to all people and which shall flourish in all ages to the end of the world; and truly, since at the present time impiety overflows not less than in the age of Noah, it is especially necessary that the waters should be restrained by this word of God, as by a thousand bolts and bars, lest they should break forth to destroy us. Wherefore, relying on this promise, Calvin says, let us look forward to the last day, in which the consuming fire shall purify heaven and earth. Although the favour which the Lord promises extends also to animals, Calvin observes, yet it is not in vain that he addresses himself only to men, who by the sense of faith are able to perceive this benefit; we enjoy the heaven and the air in common with the beasts and draw the same vital breath, but it is no common privilege that God directs his word to us, whence we may learn with what paternal love he pursues us. Here three distinct steps are to be traced, Calvin says: first, God, as in a matter of present concern, makes a covenant with Noah and his family, lest they should be afraid of a deluge for themselves; secondly, he transmits his covenant to posterity, not only that as by continual succession the effect may reach to other ages, but that they who should afterwards be born might also apprehend this testimony by faith, and might conclude that the same thing which had been promised to the sons of Noah was promised unto them; thirdly, he declares that he will be propitious also to brute animals, so that the effect of the covenant towards them might be the preservation of their lives only, without imparting to them sense and intelligence. Hence the ignorance of the Anabaptists may be refuted, Calvin says, who deny that the covenant of God is common to infants because they are destitute of present faith, as if, truly, when God promises salvation to a thousand generations, the fathers were not intermediate parties between God and their children, whose office it is to deliver to their children, so to speak, from hand to hand, the promise received from God. But as many as withdraw their life from this protection of God, since the greater part of men either despise or ridicule this divine covenant, deserve by this single act of ingratitude to be immersed in eternal fire, Calvin says; for although this be an earthly promise, yet God designs the faith of his people to be exercised, in order that they may be assured that a certain abode will by his special goodness be provided for them on earth, until they shall be gathered together in heaven.

Matthew Henry says that God is graciously pleased to deal with man in the way of a covenant, wherein God greatly magnifies his condescending favour and greatly encourages man's duty and obedience as a reasonable and gainful service; that all God's covenants with man are of his own making, which is expressed so both to raise our admiration, that though God be high yet he has this respect to man, and to confirm our assurances of the validity of the covenant; that God's covenants are established more firmly than the pillars of heaven or the foundations of the earth, and cannot be disannulled; that God's covenants are made with the covenanters and with their seed, the promise being to them and their children; and that those may be taken into covenant with God, and receive the benefits of it, who yet are not capable of restipulating or giving their own consent, for this covenant is made with every living creature, every beast of the earth. The particular intention of this covenant, Henry says, was to secure the world from another deluge: God had drowned the world once, and still it was as filthy and provoking as ever, and God foresaw the wickedness of it and yet promised he would never drown it any more, for he deals not with us according to our sins. It is owing to God's goodness and faithfulness, not to any reformation of the world, Henry says, that it has not often been deluged and that it is not deluged now; as the old world was ruined to be a monument of justice, so this world remains to this day a monument of mercy, according to the oath of God that the waters of Noah should no more return to cover the earth. This promise of God keeps the sea and clouds in their decreed place, and sets them gates and bars, Henry says: if the sea should flow but for a few days, as it does twice every day for a few hours, what desolation would it make, and how destructive would the clouds be if such showers as we have sometimes seen were continued long; but God, by flowing seas and sweeping rains, shows what he could do in wrath, and yet, by preserving the earth from being deluged between both, shows what he can do in mercy and will do in truth. This promise does not hinder, Henry adds, but that God may bring other wasting judgments upon mankind, for though he has here bound himself not to use this arrow any more, yet he has other arrows in his quiver; nor but that he may destroy particular places and countries by the inundations of the sea or rivers; nor will the destruction of the world at the last day by fire be any breach of his promise.

Charles Ellicott says the covenant between God and man is solemnly introduced as God's personal act, and that no covenant is mentioned as existing between him and the antediluvian world, but distinctly now there is a step onward in all respects, man in the renovated earth after the flood being brought nearer to God by being admitted into covenant with him. Not only is man included in the covenant, Ellicott says, but first those animals which had been with Noah in the ark, and secondly those which had not been admitted there, for the words are, from all that go out of the ark unto every beast of the earth, that is, the larger world. To such straits are those reduced who hold to the theory of a universal deluge, Ellicott says, that Kalisch argues that it means the fish, as if fishes would be destroyed by a second flood any more than they were by the first; plainly the words imply the existence of a larger world-sphere than that in connection with Noah, and give the assurance that not only those now providentially preserved, but the animals everywhere, shall never again be in danger of a similar extinction. Keil and Delitzsch print the covenant verses in full without further comment upon them.

John Wesley says we have here the general establishment of God's covenant with this new world, and the extent of that covenant. There shall not any more be a flood, he says: God had drowned the world once, and still it is as provoking as ever, yet he will never drown it any more, for he deals not with us according to our sins. This promise of God keeps the sea and clouds in their decreed place, and sets them gates and bars, Wesley says: if the sea should flow but for a few days, as it doth twice every day for a few hours, what desolations would it make, and so would the clouds, if such showers as we have sometimes seen were continued long; but God by flowing seas and sweeping rains shows what he could do in wrath, and yet by preserving the earth from being deluged between both shows what he can do in mercy, and will do in truth.

debates: What kind of covenant this is: Gill twice denies that it is the covenant of grace in Christ and calls it one of conservation, since it is made with irrational as well as rational creatures; Ellicott reads the same breadth as an advance, no covenant having existed between God and the antediluvian world, so that man is now brought nearer by being admitted into one; Henry infers that those may be taken into covenant and receive its benefits who cannot restipulate or give their own consent

Whether the covenant's reach settles the extent of the flood: Ellicott takes the phrase from all that go out of the ark unto every beast of the earth to imply a world-sphere larger than Noah's, and names Kalisch as reduced to arguing that the fish are meant in order to save the theory of a universal deluge; the others treat the promise simply as securing the world against another flood without raising the question

What follows from a covenant made with those who cannot consent: Calvin traces three steps, with Noah, with his posterity, and with the brute animals, and uses the second to refute the Anabaptists who deny that the covenant is common to infants because they lack present faith; Henry reaches the same inference from the animals themselves, that consent is not required to be taken into covenant

What the promise leaves untouched: Henry lists three limitations, that other wasting judgments may still come since God has other arrows in his quiver, that particular places may still be destroyed by inundation, and that the final destruction by fire is no breach; Calvin ends at the same place, bidding us look forward to the day when the consuming fire shall purify heaven and earth
outliers: Calvin's judgement that Noah's faith was rare and incomparable, even to a miracle, and that no strength of constancy could have been so great as not to be shaken by so terrible a vengeance
Calvin's figure of the waters restrained by this word of God as by a thousand bolts and bars, since impiety now overflows not less than in Noah's age
Gill's report from Aben Ezra that an oath was annexed to this promise, and from Jarchi that the covenant follows the exhortation to procreation as an encouragement to it
Henry's antithesis that the old world was ruined to be a monument of justice and this world remains a monument of mercy
Henry's and Wesley's shared observation that the sea flows twice every day for a few hours, and what desolation it would make if it flowed for days
Ellicott's naming of Kalisch, who is driven to read the promise of the beasts as meaning the fish

12.pericope_label: The bow set in the cloud as the token of the covenant for perpetual generations

schools.summary: Gill says the bow is what we call the rainbow, and is called a bow because of its form, being a semicircle, and a rainbow because it is seen in a day of rain and is a sign of it or of its being quickly over; it appears in a moist dewy cloud, neither very thick nor very thin, and is occasioned by the rays of the sun opposite to it, refracted on it. God calls it his bow, Gill says, not only because he made it, for notwithstanding the natural causes of it, the cloud and the sun, and the disposition of these to produce it, such a phenomenon is of God, but also because he appointed it to be a sign and token of his covenant with his creatures; so the heathen poets call the rainbow the messenger of Juno. It is a question whether there was a rainbow before the flood, Gill says, and it is not easily answered, both Jews and Christians being divided about it. Calvin says a sign is added to the promise, in which is exhibited the wonderful kindness of God, who, for the purpose of confirming our faith in his word, does not disdain to use such helps; and we must briefly maintain from these words of Moses that it is wrong to sever signs from the word. By the word, Calvin says, he means not that of which Papists boast, whereby they enchant bread, wine, water and oil with their magical whisperings, but that which may strengthen faith, according as the Lord here plainly addresses holy Noah and his sons and then annexes a seal for the sake of assurance. Wherefore, if the sacrament be wrested from the word it ceases to be what it is called, Calvin says: it must be a vocal sign in order that it may retain its force and not degenerate from its nature; and not only is that administration of sacraments in which the word of God is silent vain and ludicrous, but it draws with it pure satanic delusions. Hence we also infer that from the beginning it was the peculiar property of sacraments to avail for the confirmation of faith, Calvin says, for certainly in the covenant that promise is included to which faith ought to respond. It appears to some absurd that faith should be sustained by such helps, he adds, but they who speak thus do not reflect on the great ignorance and imbecility of our minds, nor ascribe to the working of the secret power of the Spirit that praise which is due; it is the work of God alone to begin and to perfect faith, but he does it by such instruments as he sees good, the free choice of which is in his own power. From these words certain eminent theologians have been induced to deny that there was any rainbow before the deluge, Calvin says, which is frivolous, for the words of Moses do not signify that a bow was then formed which did not previously exist, but that a mark was engraven upon it which should give a sign of the divine favour towards men. Some signs are natural and some preternatural, Calvin explains, and although there are many examples of the second class in the Scriptures, yet they are peculiar and do not belong to the common and perpetual use of the Church; as it pleases the Lord to employ earthly elements as vehicles for raising the minds of men on high, so he thinks the celestial arch, which had before existed naturally, is here consecrated into a sign and pledge, and thus a new office is assigned to it, whereas from the nature of the thing itself it might rather be a sign of the contrary, for it threatens continued rain. Let this therefore be the meaning of the words, Calvin says: as often as the rain shall alarm you, look upon the bow, for although it may seem to cause the rain to overflow the earth, it shall nevertheless be to you a pledge of returning dryness, and thus it will then become you to stand with greater confidence than under a clear and serene sky. Hence it is not for us to contend with philosophers respecting the rainbow, Calvin adds, for although its colours are the effect of natural causes, yet they act profanely who attempt to deprive God of the right and authority which he has over his creatures. Moses, by introducing God so often as the speaker, teaches us that the word holds the chief place and that signs are to be estimated by it, Calvin says; God, however, speaks after the manner of men when he says that at the sight of the rainbow he will remember his covenant, but this mode of speaking has reference to the faith of men, in order that they may reflect that God, whenever he stretches out his arch over the clouds, is not unmindful of his covenant.

Matthew Henry says that articles of agreement among men are usually sealed, that the covenants may be the more solemn and the performances the more sure, to mutual satisfaction; God therefore, being willing more abundantly to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsels, has confirmed his covenant by a seal, which makes the foundations we build on stand sure. The seal of this covenant of nature was natural enough, Henry says: it was the rainbow, which, it is likely, was seen in the clouds before, when second causes concurred, but was never a seal of the covenant till now that it was made so by a divine institution. Concerning this seal, Henry observes first that it is affixed with repeated assurances of the truth of that promise of which it was designed to be the ratification, for God says he sets his bow in the cloud, that it shall be seen in the cloud, that the eye may affect the heart and confirm the faith, that it shall be the token of the covenant, and that he will remember his covenant that the waters shall no more become a flood; nay, as if the Eternal Mind needed a memorandum, that he will look upon it that he may remember the everlasting covenant, so that here is line upon line, that we might have sure and strong consolation. Secondly, the rainbow appears when the clouds are most disposed to wet, and returns after the rain, Henry says, so that when we have most reason to fear the rain prevailing, then God shows this seal of the promise that it shall not prevail, thus obviating our fears with such encouragements as are both suitable and seasonable. Thirdly, the thicker the cloud the brighter the bow in the cloud, so that as threatening afflictions abound, encouraging consolations much more abound. Fourthly, the rainbow appears when one part of the sky is clear, which intimates mercy remembered in the midst of wrath, and the clouds are hemmed as it were with the rainbow, that they may not overspread the heavens, for the bow is coloured rain or the edges of a cloud gilded.

Charles Ellicott says the word rendered token really means sign, and is a term that has met with very unfortunate treatment in our Version, especially in the New Testament, where it is too frequently translated miracle. In the majority of the places where it occurs the sign or token is some natural occurrence, Ellicott says, but in its higher meaning it is a proof or indication of God's immediate working, so that on proper occasions it will be supernatural, because the proof of God's direct agency will most fitly be some act such as God alone can accomplish; more frequently, however, it is something natural, as the sign to the shepherds of the birth of a Saviour was their finding in a manger a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, a thing of the most simple and ordinary kind. We may dismiss, then, all such curious speculations as that no rain fell before the flood, Ellicott says, or that some condition was wanting necessary for producing this glorious symbol; what Noah needed was a guarantee and a memorial which, as often as rain occurred, would bring back to his thoughts the Divine promise, and such a memorial was best taken from the natural accompaniments of rain. We may further notice with Maimonides, Ellicott adds, that the words are not, as in our version, I do set, but my bow I have set in the cloud, that is, the bow which God set in the cloud on that day of creation in which he imposed upon air and water those laws which produce this phenomenon is now to become the sign of a solemn compact made with man by God. But a covenant is a contract between two parties, Ellicott asks, and what was the undertaking on man's part? The Talmud enumerates several of the chief moral laws which it supposes Noah was now bound to observe; more truly it was a covenant of grace, and what might have been granted simply as a promise on God's part is made into a covenant, not merely for man's greater assurance but also to indicate that it was irrevocable, since promises are revocable and their fulfilment may depend upon man's co-agency, whereas a covenant is irrevocable, and under no circumstances will the earth again be destroyed by water. Ellicott notes finally that the rainbow appears in the Chaldean Genesis, but in a heathenish manner, where the great goddess at her approach lifted up the mighty arches which Anu had created as his glory.

Adam Clarke says that on the origin and nature of the rainbow there had been a great variety of conjectures, till a bishop of Spalatro partly suggested the true cause, which was afterwards fully explained and demonstrated by Sir Isaac Newton. To readers in general it may be sufficient to say that the rainbow is a mere natural effect of a natural cause, Clarke says: it is never seen but in showery weather, nor then unless the sun shines; it never appears in any part of the heavens but in that opposite to the sun; it never appears greater than a semicircle, but often much less; it is always double, there being what is called the primary and secondary rainbow; these bows exhibit the seven prismatic colours; and the whole of the phenomenon depends on the rays of the sun falling on spherical drops of water and being, in their passage through them, refracted and reflected. The formation of the primary and secondary bow depends on two propositions, Clarke says: that when the sun shines on the drops of rain as they are falling, the rays that come from those drops to the eye of the spectator after one reflection and two refractions produce the primary rainbow, and that the rays which come after two reflections and two refractions produce the secondary. From the well-known cause of this phenomenon it cannot be rationally supposed that there was no rainbow in the heavens before the time mentioned in the text, Clarke argues, for as the rainbow is the natural effect of the sun's rays falling on drops of water it must have appeared at different times from the creation of the sun and the atmosphere; nor does the text intimate that the bow was now created for a sign to Noah and his posterity, but that what was formerly created should now be considered by them as an unfailing token of their continual preservation from the waters of a deluge. The text therefore speaks of what had already been done and not of what was now done, Clarke says, since the Hebrew reads, my bow I have given, or put, in the cloud, as if he said: as surely as the rainbow is a necessary effect of sunshine in rain, and must continue such as long as the sun and atmosphere endure, so surely shall this earth be preserved from destruction by water. Both the Greeks and Latins, as well as the Hebrews, have ever considered the rainbow as a divine token or portent, Clarke observes, and both of these nations have even deified it and made it a messenger of the gods: Homer, speaking of the figures on Agamemnon's breastplate, says there were three dragons whose colours were like to the rainbow which the son of Saturn has placed in the cloud as a sign to mankind, or to men of various languages, which some have thought is an epithet given to man from some tradition of the confusion of tongues at Babel; and Virgil twice considers the rainbow as a messenger of the gods, saying that Juno sent down the rainbow from heaven, and that Jupiter sent down the ethereal Iris. It is worthy of remark, Clarke says, that both these poets understood the rainbow to be a sign, warning or portent from heaven; and as he believes the rainbow to have been intended solely for the purpose mentioned in the text, he forbears to make spiritual uses and illustrations of it, for though many have done this, and their observations may be very edifying, they certainly have no foundation in the text. John Wesley says the rainbow, it is likely, was seen in the clouds before, but was never a seal of the covenant till now; and concerning this seal of the covenant he observes that it is affixed with repeated assurances of the truth of that promise which it was designed to be the ratification of, for God sets his bow in the cloud, it shall be seen in the cloud, it shall be a token of the covenant, and he will remember his covenant that the waters shall no more become a flood; nay, as if the eternal Mind needed a memorandum, he will look upon it that he may remember the everlasting covenant. The rainbow appears when the clouds are most disposed to wet, Wesley says, so that when we have most reason to fear the rain prevailing, God shows this seal of the promise that it shall not prevail; and it appears when one part of the sky is clear, which imitates mercy remembered in the midst of wrath, the clouds being hemmed as it were with the rainbow that it may not overspread the heavens, for the bow is coloured rain, or the edges of a cloud gilded. As God looks upon the bow that he may remember the covenant, Wesley concludes, so should we, that we also may be ever mindful of the covenant with faith and thankfulness.

debates: Whether the rainbow existed before the flood: Clarke argues from the optics that it must have appeared ever since the creation of the sun and atmosphere, and reads the Hebrew as my bow I have given; Calvin calls the contrary opinion of certain eminent theologians frivolous, holding that a mark was engraven on an arch that already existed; Ellicott dismisses the speculation and notes with Maimonides that the verb is I have set; Wesley says the bow was likely seen before but was never a seal till now; Gill alone leaves the question open, since Jews and Christians are divided

What use may lawfully be made of the sign: Clarke forbears all spiritual uses and illustrations, allowing that many have made them edifyingly but denying that they have any foundation in the text; Henry and Wesley make precisely such uses, drawing lessons from the bow's appearing in the thickest cloud and against a clear sky, and bidding us look on it as God does

What kind of thing a covenant sign is: Ellicott complains that the word is too often rendered miracle in the New Testament when it usually denotes something natural, and distinguishes a revocable promise from an irrevocable covenant; Calvin makes the occasion a doctrine of sacraments, that signs must never be severed from the word, an administration in which the word is silent being not merely vain but a satanic delusion

Why a sign that threatens rain should reassure: Calvin makes the paradox explicit, that the bow by its own nature threatens continued rain and is therefore consecrated to a new office, so that one should stand with greater confidence under it than under a serene sky; Henry and Wesley observe the same fact from the other side, that the seal is shown just when there is most reason to fear
outliers: Clarke's seven marks of the rainbow and two propositions from the optics, referred to Newton's demonstration
Clarke's classical dossier, with Homer on Agamemnon's breastplate and Virgil twice sending Iris down from heaven, and his remark that both nations deified the bow
Ellicott's citation of the Chaldean Genesis, where the goddess lifts up the mighty arches that Anu had created as his glory
Ellicott's instance of the shepherds' sign, a babe in a manger wrapped in swaddling clothes, as showing that a sign is usually something ordinary
Henry's addition that the thicker the cloud the brighter the bow, so that as afflictions abound consolations much more abound
Calvin's aside that we are not to contend with philosophers about the rainbow, since though its colours have natural causes, they act profanely who would deprive God of authority over his creatures

18.pericope_label: The three sons of Noah, and Noah plants a vineyard, drinks of the wine and is drunken

schools.summary: Gill says Noah was a man of the earth, not lord of it, as Jarchi has it, though he was, but a tiller of the earth, as he had been before the flood and now began to be again; he returned to his old employment, and perhaps improved it, having invented, as the Jews say, instruments of husbandry, and it may be the use of the plough, which made the tillage of the ground more easy. He was expert in husbandry, as Aben Ezra observes, and this is great wisdom; and though he was so great a man, yet he employed himself in this way. Of the drunkenness Gill says that either Noah was not acquainted with the strength of the wine, as many think, or he had been used to weaker liquor, as water, or it was through the infirmity of his age, but however he was overtaken with it; and this is recorded not to disgrace him but to caution men against the evil of intemperance, as well as to encourage repenting sinners to expect pardon. This shows, Gill says, that the best of men are not exempted from sin nor secure from falling, and that though Noah was a perfect man, yet not so as to be without sin, and that whereas he was a righteous man he was not so by the righteousness of works but by the righteousness of faith. Calvin says Moses enumerates the sons of Noah, not only because he is about to pass on to the following history, but for the purpose of more fully illustrating the force of the promise, Replenish the earth; for we may hence better conceive how efficacious the blessing of God has been, because an immense multitude of men proceeded in a short time from so small a number, and because one family, and that a little one, grew into so many and such numerous nations. Of the husbandry Calvin says he does not so explain the words as if Noah then for the first time began to give his attention to the cultivation of the fields, but that Moses rather intimates that Noah, with a collected mind, though now an old man, returned to the culture of the fields and to his former labours. It is uncertain whether he had been a vine-dresser or not, Calvin says: it is commonly believed that wine was not in use before that time, and this opinion has been the more willingly received as affording an honourable pretext for the excuse of Noah's sin, but it does not appear to him probable that the fruit of the vine, which excels all others, should have remained neglected and unprofitable; also Moses does not say that Noah was drunken on the first day on which he tasted it. Therefore, leaving this question undetermined, Calvin says he rather supposes that we are to learn from the drunkenness of Noah what a filthy and detestable crime drunkenness is: the holy patriarch, though he had hitherto been a rare example of frugality and temperance, losing all self-possession, did in a base and shameful manner prostrate himself naked on the ground, so as to become a laughingstock to all; therefore with what care ought we to cultivate sobriety, lest anything like this, or even worse, should happen to us. Formerly the heathen philosopher said that wine is the blood of the earth, and therefore when men intemperately pour it down their throats they are justly punished by their mother, Calvin notes; but let us rather remember that when men by shameful abuse profane this noble and most precious gift of God, he himself becomes the Avenger, and let us know that Noah, by the judgement of God, has been set forth as a spectacle to be a warning to others. Some excuse might certainly be made for the holy man, Calvin allows, who, having completed his labour and being exhilarated with wine, imagines that he is but taking his just reward; but God brands him with an eternal mark of disgrace, and what then do we suppose will happen to those idle-bellies and insatiable gluttons whose sole object of contention is who shall consume the greatest quantity of wine. And although this kind of correction was severe, Calvin adds, yet it was profitable to the servant of God, since he was recalled to sobriety, lest by proceeding in the indulgence of a vice to which he had once yielded he should ruin himself, just as we see drunkards become at length brutalised by continued intemperance.

Matthew Henry says the names of Noah's sons are again mentioned as those from whom the whole earth was overspread, by which it appears that Noah after the flood had no more children, all the world coming from these three; God, when he pleases, can make a little one to become a thousand, and greatly increase the latter end of those whose beginning was small, such being the power and efficacy of a divine blessing. The business Noah applied himself to was that of a husbandman, Henry says, that is, a man dealing in the earth, that kept ground in his hand and occupied it; we are all naturally men of the earth, made of it, living on it and hastening to it, and many are sinfully so, addicted to earthly things, but Noah was by his calling led to trade in the fruits of the earth. He began to be a husbandman, that is, some time after his departure out of the ark he returned to his old employment, from which he had been diverted by the building of the ark first, and probably afterwards by the building of a house on dry land for himself and family; for this good while he had been a carpenter, but now he began again to be a husbandman. Observe, Henry says, that though Noah was a great man and a good man, an old man and a rich man, a man greatly favoured by heaven and honoured on earth, yet he would not live an idle life, nor think the husbandman's calling below him; and though God by his providence may take us off from our callings for a time, yet when the occasion is over we should return to them.

Charles Ellicott says that though human life had begun again upon a firmer footing, yet evil and discord were soon to reappear, though in a milder form: no brother sheds a brother's blood, but in the next generation sin breaks forth afresh, and the human family is disunited thereby, the descendants of Canaan taking the place of the Cainites, without indeed their striking gifts, but nevertheless as a race foremost in trade and commerce. After enumerating the three sons of Noah, Ellicott says, we are told that from them was the whole earth overspread, that is, peopled. Of the twenty-first verse he says that he was uncovered is literally he uncovered himself, and that it was no accident but a wilful breach of modesty. Keil and Delitzsch print the narrative continuously from the naming of the sons through the vineyard, the drunkenness, the act of Ham, the covering by Shem and Japheth and the curse upon Canaan, without pausing over these verses.

Adam Clarke says the Hebrew means a man of the ground, a farmer, and that by his beginning to be a husbandman we are to understand his recommencing his agricultural operations, which undoubtedly he had carried on for six hundred years before, but which had been interrupted by the flood; and the transaction here mentioned might have occurred many years after the deluge, even after Canaan was born and grown up, for the date of it is not fixed in the text. The word husband first occurs here, Clarke says, and scarcely appears proper, because it is always applied to man in his married state; but the etymology of the term will at once show its propriety when applied to the head of a family, for husband is Anglo-Saxon and simply signifies the bond of the house or family, as by him the family is formed, united and bound together, which on his death is disunited and scattered. It is on this etymology that we can account for the farmers and petty landholders being called husbandi so early as the twelfth century, Clarke says, as appears in a statute of David the Second, king of Scotland; and the etymology appears plainer in the orthography which prevailed in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, in which he has often found the word written house-bond, as it is in a manuscript Bible before him written in the fourteenth century, though Junius disputes this etymology on what Clarke thinks no just ground. Of the drunkenness Clarke says it is very probable that this was the first time the wine was cultivated, and it is as probable that the strength or intoxicating power of the expressed juice was never before known, so that Noah might have drunk it at this time without the least blame, as he knew not till this trial the effects it would produce. He adds a case which he believes perfectly parallel and says he himself witnessed: a person who had scarcely ever heard of cider, and whose beverage through his whole life had been only milk or water, coming wet and much fatigued to a farmer's house in Somersetshire, begged for a little water or milk, and the good woman of the house, seeing him exhausted, offered him a little cider as better for him; the honest man, understanding no more of cider than that it was the simple juice of apples, drank about half a pint after some hesitation, and the consequence was that in less than half an hour he was perfectly intoxicated and could neither speak plain nor walk. A stranger to the circumstances, seeing this person, would pronounce him drunk, Clarke says, and perhaps at a third hand he might be represented as a drunkard and thus his character be blasted, while of the crime of drunkenness he was as innocent as an infant; and this Clarke presumes to have been precisely the case with Noah, so that no person, without an absolute breach of every rule of charity and candour, can attach any blame to his character on this ground, unless from a subsequent account they were well assured that, knowing the power and effects of the liquor, he had repeated the act. Some expositors seem to be glad to fix on a fact like this, Clarke complains, which by their distortion becomes a crime, and then in a strain of sympathetic tenderness they affect to deplore the failings and imperfections of the best of men, when from the interpretation that should be given of the place neither failing nor imperfection can possibly appear. John Wesley says the Hebrew means a man of the earth, a man dealing in the earth, that kept ground in his hand and occupied it, and that some time after his departure out of the ark Noah returned to his old employment, from which he had been diverted by the building of the ark first and probably after by the building of a house for himself and family. When he had gathered his vintage, Wesley supposes, probably he appointed a day of mirth and feasting in his family, and had his sons and their children with him to rejoice with him in the increase of his house as well as of his vineyard, and we may suppose he prefaced his feast with a sacrifice to the honour of God; if that was omitted, Wesley says, it was just with God to leave him to himself, to end with the beasts that did not begin with God, but we charitably hope he did. Perhaps he appointed this feast with a design in the close of it to bless his sons, as Isaac did. Of the drunkenness Wesley says it is highly probable that Noah did not know the effect of the wine before, and that he was uncovered in his tent, made naked to his shame.
