debates: Whether Noah is to be blamed for the drunkenness: Clarke exculpates him entirely, holding that the intoxicating power of the juice had never before been known, and supports it with a case of cider he says he witnessed himself; Wesley agrees that Noah probably did not know the effect beforehand; Calvin rejects the excuse at its root, since the vine can hardly have lain neglected and Moses does not say Noah was drunken on the first day he tasted it, and holds that God has branded him with an eternal mark of disgrace; Gill takes the incident as a caution that the best of men are not secure from falling

How commentators should treat such an incident: Clarke complains that some expositors are glad to fix on such a fact, which by their distortion becomes a crime, and then in a strain of sympathetic tenderness deplore the failings and imperfections of the best of men; Gill uses very nearly that formula, and Calvin makes the patriarch a spectacle set forth as a warning to others

Whether Noah's husbandry was new: Gill, Clarke, Henry and Calvin agree that he returned to an employment he had followed before the flood and had been diverted from by the building of the ark, Clarke adding that the transaction may have occurred many years after the deluge, even after Canaan was grown, since the text fixes no date

What the uncovering was: Ellicott insists the verb is reflexive, he uncovered himself, so that it was no accident but a wilful breach of modesty; Wesley says only that he was made naked to his shame, and Calvin that he prostrated himself so as to become a laughingstock to all
outliers: Clarke's Somersetshire case of a man who had drunk only milk or water, given half a pint of cider and unable within half an hour to speak plain or walk
Clarke's etymology of husband from the Anglo-Saxon for house and a verb meaning to bind, with the twelfth-century husbandi and a fourteenth-century manuscript Bible writing house-bond
Calvin's citation of the heathen philosopher that wine is the blood of the earth, so that men who pour it down intemperately are justly punished by their mother
Ellicott's forecast that the descendants of Canaan would take the place of the Cainites, foremost in trade and commerce but without their striking gifts
Gill's report from the Jews that Noah invented instruments of husbandry, and perhaps the use of the plough
Wesley's reconstruction of a vintage feast at which Noah meant to bless his sons, prefaced, as we charitably hope, with a sacrifice

22.pericope_label: Ham sees his father’s nakedness, Shem and Japheth cover him, and Canaan is cursed

schools.summary: Gill says that if Ham had seen his father's nakedness through surprise and unawares it would not have been thought criminal, but he went into his father's tent where he ought not to have entered, and looked with pleasure and delight on his father's nakedness. Ham is represented by many writers as a very wicked, immodest and profligate creature, Gill reports: Berosus makes him a magician, and the same with Zoroaster, and speaks of him as the public corrupter of mankind, saying that he taught men to live as before the flood and that he did so himself, and was therefore cast out by his father Noah and got a name signifying the infamous and immodest. Calvin says the piety as well as the modesty of the two brothers is here commended, who, in order that the dignity of their father might not be lowered in their esteem, but that they might always cherish and keep entire the reverence which they owed him, turned away their eyes from the sight of his disgrace; and thus they gave proof of the regard they paid to their father's honour, in supposing that their own eyes would be polluted if they voluntarily looked upon the nakedness by which he was disgraced. At the same time they also consulted their own modesty, Calvin says, for there is something so unaccountably shameful in the nakedness of man that scarcely any one dares to look upon himself, even when no witness is present; and they also censure the impious rashness of their brother, who had not spared his father. Hence we may learn how acceptable to God is that piety of which the example here recorded receives a signal encomium of the Spirit, Calvin says; but if piety towards an earthly father was a virtue so excellent and so worthy of praise, with how much greater devotedness of piety ought the sacred majesty of God to be worshipped? The Papists make themselves ridiculous, Calvin adds, by desiring to cover the filthiness of their idol, yea, the abominations of their whole impure clergy, with the cloak of Shem and Japheth; he omits to state how great is the difference between the disgrace of Noah and the execrable vileness of so many crimes which contaminate heaven and earth, but it is necessary that Antichrist and his horned bishops, with all that rabble, should prove themselves to be legitimate fathers if they wish that any honour should be paid them.

Matthew Henry says Noah comes to himself, for he awoke from his wine: sleep cured him, and we may suppose so cured him that he never relapsed into that sin afterwards, and those that sleep as Noah did should awake as he did, and not as that drunkard who says when he awakes that he will seek it yet again. Then the spirit of prophecy comes upon him, Henry says, and like dying Jacob he tells his sons what shall befall them. He pronounces a curse on Canaan the son of Ham, in whom Ham is himself cursed, either because this son of his was now more guilty than the rest, or because the posterity of this son was afterwards to be rooted out of their land to make room for Israel; and Moses here records it for the animating of Israel in the wars of Canaan, since though the Canaanites were a formidable people, yet they were of old an accursed people and doomed to ruin. The particular curse is that he shall be a servant of servants, Henry says, that is, the meanest and most despicable servant, even to his brethren, so that those who by birth were his equals shall by conquest be his lords; and this certainly points at the victories obtained by Israel over the Canaanites, by which they were all either put to the sword or put under tribute, which happened not till about eight hundred years after this. God often visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, Henry adds, especially when the children inherit the fathers' wicked dispositions and imitate their wicked practices.

Charles Ellicott says the phrase rendered his younger son is in Hebrew his son, the little one, and can only mean his youngest son, being so applied to Benjamin and to David; now Ham was not the youngest son but Japheth, and it is not Ham who is cursed but Canaan. So far from Ham being accursed, Ellicott says, his descendants were building mighty cities such as Egyptian Thebes, Nineveh and Babylon, were rearing palaces, digging canals, organising governments and founding empires at a time when the descendants of Japheth were wandering over Europe with no better weapons than implements of flint and bone. The application of the curse to Ham seems to have been suggested to commentators by the degradation of the African race in modern times, and especially by the prevalence of negro slavery, Ellicott says, but anciently the converse was the case, and for centuries the Egyptians, a Hamite race, made the Israelites serve them; we must not extend, therefore, to Ham the curse pronounced upon Canaan. But what had Canaan done to deserve it, he asks: as the son, the little one, was not Ham, so certainly it was not Japheth, but probably it was Canaan, who was the youngest son of Ham, and since in Hebrew son is occasionally used for grandson he might be described as Noah's youngest son, being the youngest member of his family. Origen quotes a tradition that Canaan was the first who saw Noah's exposure and that he told it to his father, Ellicott notes, and Aben Ezra says that Canaan had done worse than mock, though the Scripture does not in words reveal his crime; with some such surmise we must be content. The prophecy of Noah takes the form of a poem, Ellicott says, and in it Ham is passed over in silence, as though his unfilial conduct made him unworthy of a blessing while it was not so wicked as to bring on him a curse, the whole weight of Noah's displeasure falling on Canaan, whose degraded position among the nations is thrice insisted upon. A servant of servants means the most abject of slaves, Ellicott says, which was fulfilled in the conquest of Canaan by Joshua; but the race had nevertheless a great future before it, the Hittites being one of the foremost nations of antiquity, and the Sidonians, Tyrians and Phoenicians such famous traders that Canaanite is in our version translated merchant, without even a note in the margin. But the whole race was enslaved by one of the most terrible and degrading forms of idolatry, Ellicott says, and as Shem's blessing is religious, so possibly is Canaan's curse; he quotes Lenormant, that no other people ever rivalled them in the mixture of bloodshed and debauchery with which they thought to honour the Deity, and Creuzer, that the Canaanite religion silenced all the best feelings of human nature and degraded men's minds by a superstition alternately cruel and profligate.

Adam Clarke says there is no occasion to enter into any detail, the sacred text being circumstantial enough: Ham, and very probably his son Canaan, had treated their father on this occasion with contempt or reprehensible levity, whereas the conduct of Shem and Japheth was such as became pious and affectionate children, who appear to have been in the habit of treating their father with decency, reverence and obedient respect. Had Noah not been innocent, as his exposition supposes him, Clarke argues, God would not have endued him with the spirit of prophecy on this occasion and testified such marked disapprobation of their conduct. On the one the spirit of prophecy, not the incensed father, pronounces a curse, Clarke says, and on the others the same spirit, not parental tenderness, pronounces a blessing; these things had been just as they afterwards occurred had Noah never spoken, since God had wise and powerful reasons to induce him to sentence the one to perpetual servitude and to allot to the others prosperity and dominion. Besides, the curse pronounced on Canaan neither fell immediately upon himself nor on his worthless father, but upon the Canaanites, Clarke says; and from the history we have of that people we may ask, could the curse of God fall more deservedly on any people than on these? Their profligacy was great, but it was not the effect of the curse; but, being foreseen by the Lord, the curse was the effect of their conduct. Even this curse does not exclude them from the possibility of obtaining salvation, Clarke insists: it extends not to the soul and to eternity, but merely to their bodies and to time, though if they continued to abuse their liberty and refuse to be saved on God's terms, then the wrath of divine justice must come upon them to the uttermost; how many even of these repented, we cannot tell. Of the curse itself Clarke notes that in the twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh verses the Arabic version has Ham the father of Canaan instead of Canaan simply, but that this is acknowledged by none of the other versions and seems to be merely a gloss. John Wesley says that to have seen his father's nakedness accidentally and involuntarily would not have been a crime, but Ham pleased himself with the sight, and that he told his two brethren without, in the street, as the word is, in a scornful deriding manner. A servant of servants means the meanest and most despicable servant, Wesley says, even to his brethren, so that those who by birth were his equals should by conquest be his lords; this certainly points at the victories obtained by Israel over the Canaanites, by which they were all either put to the sword or put under tribute, which happened not till about eight hundred years after this. God often visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, Wesley adds, especially when the children inherit the fathers' wicked dispositions and imitate the fathers' wicked practices.

debates: Whether the curse on Canaan falls on Ham: Henry says Canaan is cursed and in him Ham is himself cursed, either as the more guilty son or because his posterity was to be rooted out for Israel; Ellicott denies the transfer, arguing from the phrase his son, the little one, that Ham was not the youngest, and pointing to Hamite cities and empires raised while Japheth's descendants wandered Europe with flint and bone; he adds that the application of the curse to Ham seems to have been suggested to commentators by the modern degradation of the African race and the prevalence of negro slavery, whereas anciently the Egyptians made Israel serve them

What Canaan had done: Ellicott supposes he was himself the offender, citing a tradition in Origen that Canaan first saw the exposure and told his father, and Aben Ezra's opinion that he had done worse than mock; Clarke thinks Ham and very probably Canaan both treated their father with contempt; Gill collects the older charges against Ham himself, including the identification with Zoroaster

Whether the curse is paternal anger or prophecy: Clarke insists it is the spirit of prophecy and not the incensed father that speaks, and that these things would have occurred just as they did had Noah never spoken, the Canaanites' profligacy being the cause of the foreseen curse rather than its effect; Henry likewise calls it the spirit of prophecy, comparing dying Jacob

How far the curse reaches: Clarke limits it strictly, holding that it fell on the Canaanites and not on Canaan or Ham personally, and that it extends not to the soul and to eternity but merely to their bodies and to time, leaving the possibility of salvation open; Ellicott grounds it in the people's religion rather than their blood, and balances it against the great future of the Hittites and the Tyrian traders

What the text says of the reading of the versions: Clarke notes that the Arabic has Ham the father of Canaan in all three verses of the oracle, but rejects it as a gloss unsupported by any other version
outliers: Gill's report from Berosus that Ham was a magician, the same as Zoroaster, and the public corrupter of mankind, who got a name signifying the infamous and immodest
Calvin's remark that there is something so unaccountably shameful in man's nakedness that scarcely any one dares look upon himself even when no witness is present

Calvin's charge that the Papists make themselves ridiculous in covering the abominations of their clergy with the cloak of Shem and Japheth, and that Antichrist and his horned bishops must first prove themselves fathers
Ellicott's citation of Lenormant, that no other people rivalled the Canaanites in the mixture of bloodshed and debauchery with which they thought to honour the Deity
Ellicott's note that Canaanite is rendered merchant in our version without even a marginal note, so famous were the Sidonian and Tyrian traders
Henry's observation that sleep cured Noah, and we may suppose so cured him that he never relapsed into that sin afterwards

26.pericope_label: Blessed be the God of Shem, God enlarge Japheth, and the death of Noah

schools.summary: Gill says Shem was blessed before Japheth because he was the first and principal in advising and conducting the affair before ascribed to them, as Jarchi suggests; and though the words are in the form of an ascription of blessedness to God, the fountain of all good, and by whose grace Shem was influenced and enabled to do the good he did, yet it includes the blessing of Shem, and indeed the greatest blessing he could possibly enjoy, for what greater blessing is there than for a man to have God to be his God? This includes everything, all blessings temporal and spiritual, Gill says; and some interpret the God of Shem of Christ, who according to the human nature was a descendant of Shem, and according to the divine nature the God of Shem, God over all, blessed for ever. Calvin says Noah blesses his other children, but in a different manner, for he places Shem in the highest post of honour; and this is the reason why Noah, in blessing him, breaks forth in the praise of God, without adhering to the person of man, since the Hebrews, when they are speaking of any rare and transcendent excellence, raise their thoughts to God. Therefore the holy man, when he perceived that the most abundant grace of God was destined for his son Shem, rises to thanksgiving, Calvin says; whence we infer that he spoke not from carnal reason, but rather treated of the secret favours of God, the result of which was to be deferred to a remote period; and finally, by these words it is declared that the benediction of Shem would be divine or heavenly. Of the closing verses Calvin says that although Moses briefly states the age of the holy man, and does not record the memorable events of his life, yet those things which are certain, and which Scripture elsewhere commemorates, ought to recur to our minds. Within one hundred and fifty years, Calvin says, the offspring of his three sons became so numerous that he had sufficient and even abundant proof of the efficacy of the divine benediction, Increase and multiply: he sees not one city only filled with his grandchildren, nor his seed expanded barely to three hundred families, but many nations springing from one of his sons who should inhabit extensive regions; and this astonishing increase, since it was a visible representation of the divine favour towards him, would doubtless fill him with unbounded joy. In the meantime, however, Calvin says, he was compelled to behold many things which would afflict his holy breast with incredible grief: to omit other things, he saw in the family of Shem the sanctuary of God, into which the sons of Japheth were to be received, destroyed, or at least dilapidated and rent, for whereas the father of Abraham himself, having deserted his proper station, had erected for himself a profane tabernacle, a very small portion indeed remained of those who worshipped God in the harmonious consent of a pure faith. With what tormenting pains this terrible confusion affected him cannot be sufficiently expressed in words, Calvin says; hence we may know that his eyes of faith must have been exceedingly penetrating, which did not fail to behold afar off the grace of God in preserving the Church, at that time overwhelmed by the wickedness of men. Calvin's editor notes that Abraham was nearly fifty years old when his ancestor Noah died, and that while Lightfoot places the death of Noah two years before the birth of Abraham, Clarke places it two years after, though these chronological differences do not materially affect the conclusion.

Matthew Henry says we may see here how God prolonged the life of Noah, who lived nine hundred and fifty years, twenty more than Adam and but nineteen less than Methuselah; this long life was a further reward of his signal piety, and a great blessing to the world, to which no doubt he continued a preacher of righteousness, with this advantage, that now all he preached to were his own children. We may see also how God put a period to his life at last, Henry says: though he lived long, yet he died, having probably first seen many that descended from him dead before him. Noah lived to see two worlds, Henry concludes, but, being an heir of the righteousness which is by faith, when he died he went to see a better than either.

Charles Ellicott says the greatness of Shem's blessing is shown by its taking the form of a hymn of praise to Jehovah, the personal God, and that the patriarch's fervent outburst of thanksgiving was a presage of the hallelujahs that were to arise unto God from all mankind for the birth of that son of Shem in whom all nations were to be blessed; the following words, he adds, should be translated, and let Canaan be their servant, the servant both of Shem and Japheth. Of the next verse Ellicott says that first the Deity is here Elohim, following upon Jehovah in the preceding verse, and that with extraordinary exactness: Jehovah has never been the special name of the Deity worshipped by the race of Japheth, though doubtless it is the Greek Zeus and the Latin Jove, but it soon became the proper title of God in covenant with the race of Shem; it is plainly impossible, therefore, to divide this most ancient poem into Elohistic and Jehovistic sections, and the theory, however plausible occasionally, fails in a crucial place like this. Next, Ellicott says, there is a play upon the name of Japheth, our translators having made the same mistake as in changing Hebel into Abel, for the Hebrew is God enlarge the enlarger, and not God shall enlarge. While it is the special blessing of Shem that through him the voice of thanksgiving is to ascend to Jehovah, the God of grace, Ellicott says, it is Elohim, the God of nature and of the universe, who gives to Japheth wide extension and the most numerous posterity; and if the most ancient civilisation and the earliest empires in Egypt and on the Tigris were Hamite, the great world-powers of history, the Chaldean, the Medo-Persian, the Greek and Roman, the Hindoo, were all of Japhetic origin, as are also the modern rulers of mankind. In one sense Shem now dwells in the tents of Japheth, Ellicott says, for the Jews, the noblest representatives of Shem, dwell dispersed in Aryan countries, and except in the Arabian peninsula the Shemites have no home of their own; but the religious privileges of their race now belong to the family of Japheth, carried by Jewish missionaries like St Paul throughout the Roman world, and thus Japheth takes possession of the tents which by right of primogeniture belonged to Shem, for to dwell in the tents of Shem is not so much to share them as to own them. If the Jews retain some degree of faith, Ellicott says, it has lost with them all expansive power, while the right interpretation of their Scriptures, and as well the maintenance as the propagation of the religion of their Messiah, are now in the hands of the descendants of Japheth; yet Shem does not lose all pre-eminence, for if he loses the foremost place of primogeniture he is still a brother, and Canaan but a slave. Of the last verse Ellicott says that while Noah attained to the same age as the antediluvian patriarchs, nine hundred and fifty years, human life was fast diminishing: the whole lifetime of Shem was six hundred years, that of Peleg, a few generations afterwards, only two hundred and thirty-nine, and after him only one man, Terah, is described as living more than two hundred years, and of his age there is great doubt; thus before Shem's death the age of man was rapidly shortening, and things were settling down to that condition in which they are set before us in profane literature. Keil and Delitzsch say that, starting from the meaning of the name, Noah sums up his blessing in a word meaning to be wide, used in this form of procuring a wide space for anyone, either of extension over a wide territory or of removal to a free and unfettered position; both must be retained here, so that the promise to the family of Japheth embraced not only a wide extension but also prosperity on every hand. This blessing was desired by Noah, Keil says, not from Jehovah, the God of Shem, who bestows saving spiritual good upon man, but from Elohim, God as Creator and Governor of the world, for it had respect primarily to the blessings of the earth and not to spiritual blessings, although Japheth would participate in these as well, since he should come and dwell in the tents of Shem. Keil then raises the disputed question of who is to dwell in those tents, but the block breaks off before the answer.

Adam Clarke says Noah was the oldest patriarch on record except Methuselah and Jared, and quotes Dr Hales on the three families. Ham signifies burnt or black, Hales says, and this name was peculiarly significant of the regions allotted to his family: to the Cushites were allotted the hot southern regions of Asia along the coasts of the Persian Gulf, to the sons of Canaan Palestine and Syria, and to the sons of Misraim Egypt and Libya; the Hamites in general were a seafaring race and sooner arrived at civilisation and the luxuries of life than their simpler pastoral and agricultural brethren, the first great empires of Assyria and Egypt being founded by them and the republics of Sidon, Tyre and Carthage being early distinguished for their commerce, but they sooner also fell to decay. Shem signifies name or renown, Hales continues, and his indeed was great in a temporal and spiritual sense, the finest regions of Upper and Middle Asia being allotted to his family; but the chief renown of Shem was of a spiritual nature, since he was destined to be the lineal ancestor of the blessed seed of the woman, and to this glorious privilege Noah, to whom it was probably revealed, might have alluded in that devout ejaculation, Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem. The pastoral life of the Shemites is strongly marked in the prophecy by the tents of Shem, Hales says, and such it remains to the present day throughout their midland settlements in Asia. Japheth signifies enlargement, he adds, and how wonderfully did Providence enlarge his boundaries: his posterity diverged eastward and westward throughout the whole extent of Asia north of the great range of Taurus, whence they probably crossed over to America by Behring's Straits from Kamtschatka, and in the opposite direction throughout Europe to the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, from whence also they might have crossed over to America by Newfoundland; thus did they gradually enlarge themselves till they literally encompassed the earth within the precincts of the northern temperate zone. Their hardy race and enterprising, warlike genius made them frequently encroach southwards on the settlements of Shem, whose pastoral and agricultural occupations rendered them more inactive and unwarlike, Hales says, and so they dwelt in the tents of Shem when the Scythians invaded Media, and when the Greeks and afterwards the Romans overran and subdued the Assyrians, Medes and Persians in the east, and the Syrians and Jews in the south. John Wesley says that all blessings are included in the God of Shem, this being the blessing conferred on Abraham and his seed, of whom the God of heaven was not ashamed to be called their God; Shem is sufficiently recompensed for his respect to his father by this, that the Lord himself puts this honour upon him to be his God, which is a sufficient recompense for all our services and all our sufferings for his name. Of the next verse Wesley says the seed of Japheth shall be so numerous and so victorious that they shall be masters of the tents of Shem, which was fulfilled when the people of the Jews, the most eminent of Shem's race, were tributaries to the Grecians first and after to the Romans, both of Japheth's seed. This also speaks the conversion of the Gentiles and the bringing of them into the church, Wesley says, and then we should read it, God shall persuade Japheth, for so the word signifies, and being so persuaded he shall dwell in the tents of Shem, that is, Jews and Gentiles shall be united together in the gospel fold; after many of the Gentiles shall have been proselyted to the Jewish religion, both shall be one in Christ. When Japheth joins with Shem, Wesley concludes, Canaan falls before them both: when strangers become friends, enemies become servants.

debates: What dwelling in the tents of Shem means: Ellicott makes it possession rather than hospitality, holding that the religious privileges of Shem's race now belong to Japheth, carried there by Jewish missionaries, and that whatever faith the Jews retain has lost all expansive power; Wesley gives the verb two senses, reading it of enlargement fulfilled when the Jews were tributary to Greeks and Romans, and also of persuasion, so that Jews and Gentiles are united in the gospel fold

Why the divine name changes between the two blessings: Keil says Noah asked Japheth's blessing not of Jehovah, the God of Shem, who bestows saving spiritual good, but of Elohim, God as Creator and Governor, since it had respect primarily to the blessings of the earth; Ellicott makes the same observation and turns it into an argument that this most ancient poem cannot be divided into Elohistic and Jehovistic sections, the theory failing in a crucial place

Why Shem's blessing is worded as praise to God rather than to Shem: Gill says it nonetheless includes the greatest blessing a man can have, that God should be his God; Calvin explains it as the Hebrew habit of raising the thoughts to God when speaking of transcendent excellence, and infers that Noah was treating of secret favours deferred to a remote period; Ellicott makes the hymn-form itself the measure of the blessing's greatness

How Noah's last centuries are to be imagined: Henry makes them a reward of his piety and supposes he continued a preacher of righteousness, now to his own children only; Calvin sets the joy of a numerous posterity against the grief of seeing the sanctuary in Shem's family dilapidated, since Abraham's own father had erected a profane tabernacle
